GLOF / GLACIAL LAKE OUTBURST FLOOD

A natural dam.
A sudden release.

A GLOF happens when water rapidly escapes a glacial lake. Breaching, overtopping, or failure of its natural barrier can send water, sediment, and boulders down a valley toward communities and infrastructure.[1]

01 / THE LONG-TERM DRIVER

A warmer climate

Glacier melt and retreat leave basins where meltwater collects. Existing lakes can enlarge as glaciers lose ice.[1]

Lake formation + growth
02 / THE WEATHER STRESS

Rain & melt extremes

Heavy or changing rainfall and snowmelt can increase inflow and stress lake barriers. Irregular rain is a risk context, rather than a universal explanation for lake formation.[2]

Water input + hazard context
03 / THE FRAGILE BARRIER

Unstable natural dams

Loose moraine sediment and ice can erode or fail. Seepage may weaken a barrier from within.[1]

Breach susceptibility
04 / THE SUDDEN TRIGGER

Avalanches & slope failure

Rock or ice entering a lake can create a displacement wave that overtops its dam and triggers a flood cascade.[3]

Outburst trigger
WHY THE DISTINCTION MATTERS

Lake formation, dam failure, and downstream exposure are different parts of the problem. A bigger lake alone does not prove an outburst is imminent.

The goal is time
to make a safer decision.

Earlier, trusted warnings can give downstream residents time to move away from exposed areas and allow local authorities to activate response plans. Effective warnings also need reliable communications, practiced evacuation routes, and people who can act.

GLOFJev’s intended impact: improve monitoring and review. Lives saved and evacuation lead time have not been measured for this prototype.

Working code, with evidence to show

The supplied notebooks implement cloud-aware area measurements, per-lake baselines, contextual checks, exports, and Qwen classifier training. Demonstrate a real scene and its saved result to verify the connected runtime.

What makes a warning actionable

Satellite revisit and cloud gaps limit freshness. Rapid evacuation warning requires ground sensors, hydrological routing, dependable communications, and an authorized response team. Those are future operational integrations.

The intelligence behind the decision

Decisions without
the long conversation.

JEV motivates a useful pattern: turn a measured state into a bounded decision. GLOFJev explores that pattern with a local Qwen-based classifier.

TRAINABLE DECISION LAYER

A small classification head

Learned feature → class mapping

decision_output: future-onset class
scores: model class scores
review: evidence + human judgment

Architecture from your training notebook. Class scores require calibration before they can be interpreted as operational probabilities.

01 /

Fast by design

The classifier produces a class output instead of generating a long answer. Caching Qwen representations makes repeated head training inexpensive. Live inference still runs the backbone and needs a measured latency benchmark.

02 /

Lower recurring API cost

The local model needs no hosted JEV API call. A frozen backbone and small trainable head reduce training work; EC2 compute, storage, and data transfer still have costs.

03 /

Learned decision intelligence

The head can learn relationships across lake change and context features rather than relying on a single threshold. Its ability to generalize depends on representative labels and validation.

04 /

Accuracy that can be evaluated

A fixed set of outputs makes class-level errors inspectable. Measure event recall, false alarms, calibration, and lead time on held-out real lakes and events before claiming forecasting accuracy.

TypeSafe’s JEV · the inspirationA proprietary System One model with typed decisions. TypeSafe reports 70–500 ms responses and $0.042 per million input tokens in its launch post. These are vendor-reported figures for JEV, and do not benchmark our model.[7]

Qwen-JEV · what this project usesA locally trained, JEV-inspired classifier adapted from Anubhab Banerjee’s tutorial. It uses Qwen representations plus a linear head. It does not reproduce TypeSafe’s architecture, calibrated-decision training, or hosted service.

Current evidence: the supplied training notebook includes 720 synthetic examples for software testing. Scores on those examples demonstrate the training workflow; they do not establish real-world GLOF prediction accuracy or lives saved.

Final three-minute recording script

Read the narration; follow the screen cues. These six beats match presentation mode and reserve the final 15 seconds for your thank-you page. Rehearse the complete recording within three minutes, including screen changes. The working-feature and AWS paragraphs accompany your actual recorded run.

0:00–0:25The problem and the people

On screen: Show the glacier-to-lake diagram. Move through formation, growth and breach while introducing the downstream audience.

Hi, I’m Devesh Kumar, and this is GLOFJev. A glacial lake outburst flood happens when a lake suddenly releases water downstream. Glacier retreat can create or enlarge lakes, while heavy rainfall, unstable barriers and slope failures can increase the risk. We aim to help researchers and disaster-management teams monitor these lakes and prepare downstream communities.

0:25–0:50A warning that reached someone

On screen: Show the teacher clipping and the two student figures. Keep the full headline visible; explain the evacuated-versus-enrolled distinction.

This teacher’s story shows why warnings matter. In Nepal, Rajendra Dawadi received warnings and moved about nine hundred students uphill before floodwater swept away their school. Reports distinguish nine hundred evacuated from sixteen hundred and forty-three enrolled. This flood-evacuation case shows the value of timely information, a clear route and someone ready to act.

0:50–1:45One observation through the workflow

On screen: Introduce the four stages, then switch to your actual pipeline and dashboard recording. Show the scene date, DeepLab mask, measured area, saved record and matching result. Use pauses to point out each output. The showcase’s preset scenarios are illustrative.

Our workflow has four stages: collect observations, identify the lake, measure change and support review. Here is the actual satellite scene and its acquisition time. DeepLab segments the lake, then the pipeline measures its area and stores that observation. The dashboard lets a reviewer inspect the result alongside historical, weather and seismic context. We want changes to be easier to notice and assess. Satellite monitoring has cloud and revisit limits, so ground sensing and reliable local communication are also needed for rapid evacuation warnings.

1:45–2:20Why a JEV-inspired decision layer

On screen: Return to the JEV section. Point to the frozen Qwen representations, small classifier and bounded review label. Add latency or accuracy numbers only if you have measured them.

Our decision layer uses a local Qwen model inspired by JEV. Its learned representations feed a small classifier, producing a clear review label instead of a long generated answer. This design is intended to reduce response time and decision cost. Accuracy still needs independent testing on real events; synthetic training scores alone cannot establish forecasting performance. Every result remains subject to expert review.

2:20–2:45AWS execution and tools used

On screen: Switch to actual AWS footage: identify the service, show the running process, execute one request, and match logs to the dashboard result. Show S3 only if used. Read this paragraph alongside that recorded evidence; an architecture diagram cannot establish execution.

Here is the AWS execution: the running backend, one processing request, its logs and the matching dashboard result. This shows where cloud compute fits in the workflow. We used ChatGPT and Codex for research, code assistance and preparing this showcase.

2:45–3:00Thank you — Devesh Kumar

On screen: Return to the thank-you page. Keep your name, second-year CSE details and IIIT Delhi logo on screen through the final sentence.

Thank you for watching. I’m Devesh Kumar, a second-year Computer Science and Engineering student at IIIT Delhi. GLOFJev aims to support earlier review and better preparedness for downstream communities.
